claims.text: A multi-stage adaptive thermodynamic-integration protocol can produce faithful free energies for both solid and liquid states near fusion.
The proposed protocol can retain vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration entropy contributions.
The proposed protocol can operate at a fraction of the computational cost of explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
Low-cost empirical or machine-learned potential-energy surfaces will be used for initial phase-space sampling.
Sampled ensembles will be reweighted using targeted ab initio corrections in critical regions.
Adaptive switching between replica exchange and reweighting will minimize expensive ab initio sampling cycles.
Multiple entropy contributions materially affect phase stability in high-entropy alloys.
The cited prior methods have been validated for elemental or binary systems near melting.
Efficiently bridging a low-cost potential-energy surface to an ab initio landscape will preserve the relevant fusion free-energy contributions.
Low-cost presampling followed by selective ab initio refinement will reduce the number of expensive simulation steps.
Reweighting will accurately capture entropy contributions across phase transitions.
The protocol will match explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free energies within chemical-accuracy margins.
The protocol will provide a several-fold speedup relative to full ab initio molecular dynamics.
The protocol will outperform TOR-TILD particularly for multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy evaluations are highly accurate but computationally very costly.
TOR-TILD exhibits decreased performance in complex compositional spaces.
The intended domain extends from elemental and binary systems to multicomponent high-entropy alloys near their melting points.
Preliminary results in simpler systems and selected binary evaluations suggest that the proposed strategy will succeed.
A benchmark on identical thermodynamic states can compare solid and liquid phase free energies, entropy contributions, and computational cost against explicit ab initio calculations.
The hypothesis is falsified by errors exceeding kBT per atom or by a speedup below 2× relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.

contradictions.description: The predicted fidelity is stated as chemical accuracy, but the proposed error threshold is kBT per atom. Near melting, kBT per atom can be substantially larger than the conventional chemical-accuracy scale, so a result could violate the predicted fidelity without meeting the stated falsification criterion.
